content.rendered:
It was their first international single, and it was the last song they ever performed live. And other than “New Sensation” (which just barely edged it out), it was the song they performed the most.

INXS had other songs that could lay claim to being their signature, but “Don’t Change” has a pretty good case to make for being their anthem.

“Don’t Change” was the second single from the band’s 1982 Shabooh Shabooh album, and although it didn’t actually perform as well as “The One Thing” (peaking only at #80 on the Billboard Hot 100), it was the song that cemented their international arrival.

Both lyrically and musically simple, “Don’t Change” was nevertheless an electrifying performance and production–all of which makes it a very attractive song for musicians to cover. (“It’s a good pub band song,” co-writer Andrew Farris told Songfacts.com. “You don’t have to know too many chords to play it.”)

So when Bruce Springsteen decided to pay tribute to the late Michael Hutchence when he played Hutchence’s home town of Sydney in 2014, “Don’t Change” was an obvious choice. But who would have guessed the super-sized E Street Band would be so well-suited to the song?

Wisely calling upon the E Street Horns to carry the iconic synth riff from the original, and featuring some positively furious guitars, “Don’t Change” sounded fresh and urgent, easily cementing itself as one of Bruce’s best modern covers.

How furious and urgent, you ask?

Well, let’s just say Bruce and the band were on such an adrenaline rush after covering “Don’t Change” that they barreled into and through the fastest, most electric “Born to Run” in modern memory immediately after–something Bruce noticed immediately. (Check out his comment at about 10:50 below.)

Don’t Change
First performed: February 19, 2014 (Sydney, Australia)
Last performed: May 13, 2014 (Albany, NY)

© March 26, 2021

excerpt.rendered: When Bruce and the E Street Band visited INXS’s home town of Sydney in 2014, they paid tribute with one of their very best modern covers.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Chimes of Freedom
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: When Bruce announced his participation in the Amnesty International Human Rights Now! Tour in 1988, his re-arrangement and performance of this Bob Dylan classic became the title track of an EP released the following month.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Run Through the Jungle
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: A quiet, taut take on the CCR anti-gun classic rocker. "200 millions guns are loaded..." If only.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Cover Me: Any Other Way
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Even Bruce Springsteen's musical encyclopedia can miss an entry or two, as evidenced by his adaptation of this William Bell song transformed by Jackie Shane.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Running on Empty
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: A contemporary contrast to "Born to Run," Jackson Browne's classic road song begs for a Jackson/Bruce team-up. Let's check out a couple of them inside.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Cover Me: Don’t Play That Song (You Lied)
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Who'd have thought a 60-year-old "Stand By Me" clone would become a fan-favorite centerpiece on tour?

jetpack-related-posts.title: Signed, Sealed, Delivered I’m Yours
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: One time only: John Legend, India Arie, Billy Joel, and Bruce Springsteen join forces on an anticipatory, celebratory cover of Stevie Wonder's 1970 classic.
